title: The flute and the song offerings
hookLine: a small reed flute, carried over hills, played by someone else's breath
carry: bhakti: we offer god what god gave first
tomorrow: God in the dust of the road

lines: A REED FLUTE MAKES NO SOUND ALONE.
cards: A reed flute is a plain thing. A hollow stalk, a few holes, nothing inside. It makes no sound on its own; somebody has to breathe through it.
In 1912, a Bengali poet came to London with English versions of his own songs. The Irish poet W. B.

Yeats read them, wrote the introduction, and the book came out that year with the subtitle Song Offerings. The next year its author became the first writer from outside Europe to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.
The poet is Rabindranath Tagore. The book is Gitanjali, and its first poem is about that flute.

teach.b: Here is how the first poem opens, in Tagore's own English: "Thou hast made me endless, such is thy pleasure. This frail vessel thou emptiest again and again, and fillest it ever with fresh life."
Then the flute: this little reed has been carried over hills and dales, and thou has breathed through it melodies always new. The singer doesn't make the music. He's the instrument.
That flips the title around. A song offering sounds like a gift a person makes and hands up to God. Here the songs were breathed in from the other side first, and what's offered back was given.
That is the heart of bhakti, loving devotion.

teach.h: A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.
teach.b: In the Gita, Krishna says: offer me a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, with love, and I accept it. The leaf and the fruit were never ours to begin with.
At home shrines and in temples, families offer food to God, then take it back as prasad: the same food, now a gift returned.
Tagore's poem ends on hands: the infinite gifts come only on these very small hands, ages pass, and still thou pourest, and still there is room to fill.
He never names a god here; some readers hear Krishna, always pictured with a flute. Either way the bhakti question for a gift you give today, a meal, a song, a day's work, isn't how much did I make.
It's what was I given, that I'm handing back.

how: Many Hindus offer food to God at a home shrine or temple and receive it back as prasad; Tagore's Gitanjali songs, first written in Bengali, are still sung at home, in schools and at gatherings in Bengal.

o: a collection of the Gita's verses set to new music
a Bengali epic about a prince who wins back a kingdom
a poet's song offerings, given back to the one who breathed them in

games.q: Gitanjali and the offering — tap the pairs.
p: emptied and filled with fresh life
a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water
food offered to God, given back

s: in poem one, the singer fills himself with life
the vessel is emptied and filled by the one he calls thou.
the poem pictures the singer as a flute someone else breathes through
a little reed carried over hills and dales, playing melodies always new.
prasad is food given up to God and never eaten
it's offered to God, then received back and shared as a gift.

games.q: you're setting a plate of fruit at the home shrine. in bhakti, whose fruit is it?
o: God's first. you offer it back, and it returns as prasad.
games.why: in Tagore's first poem the singer is a flute God breathes through, and in the Gita Krishna accepts a leaf or a fruit offered with love. what's offered was given first, and comes back as prasad.

practice: Let your hands rest open in your lap, palms up: small hands. Breathe out fully, then let the next breath come in on its own, and notice that you didn't make it; it arrived.

Now bring to mind one thing you'll give today, a meal, a song, a piece of work. If you pray, offer it in your own words to the one you pray to, as a gift returned; if not, just notice what in it was given to you first.

wordCard.voice: Tagore's Gitanjali. Song offerings from a poet who pictures himself as a flute: what he gives back to God was breathed into him first.

orig.note: Bengali, the language Tagore wrote the songs in. The English edition's subtitle is Song Offerings.

carryVoice: Your line: bhakti: we offer God what God gave first. Tomorrow, a temple with its doors shut. See you there.
